content: The data indicates that certain countries, particularly in Eastern Europe, report higher rates of transfusion of specific blood components, such as fresh frozen plasma, per 1,000 population. This may suggest suboptimal utilization of blood products. To address this, detailed studies, including clinical audits and reviews of transfusion data, should be conducted at national and subnational levels. These efforts can help assess the current situation, update national guidelines, and improve transfusion practices. The responsibility for ensuring a safe and adequate blood supply lies with governments. Blood services should be integrated into national healthcare policies and infrastructure. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that countries establish policies, systems, and structures to ensure the safety, quality, accessibility, and timely availability of blood and blood products for all patients requiring transfusion. These policies should be supported by appropriate legislation and regulatory frameworks to ensure consistent implementation of standards and quality control. Many developing countries, particularly in the WHO African and South-East Asia regions, have reported having national blood policies and strategic plans, reflecting governmental commitment to improving blood safety and supply adequacy. The European region has the highest number of countries with legislation supporting their blood policies, while other regions, including Africa and South-East Asia, report lower percentages of countries with specific legislation. However, several countries in these regions have policies and plans in place. Effective implementation of these policies requires supportive systems, such as functioning national committees, to ensure tangible outcomes. Globally, most countries have national standards for the collection, testing, processing, storage, and distribution of blood and blood components, which are essential for a quality blood transfusion system. However, outside of Europe, fewer countries report having mechanisms for quality oversight, monitoring, or programs to enforce standards and maintain quality systems. There is an urgent need to establish sustainable quality systems and strengthen regulatory and oversight capacities in many countries. Governments must ensure adequate and sustainable financing for national blood programs, integrating this into the financial structure of national healthcare systems through mechanisms such as budget allocations, cost recovery, and health insurance. Insufficient funding for blood services hampers efforts to improve blood safety, particularly in developing countries. Many lowand lower-middle-income countries rely heavily on external donors for funding, which should gradually be replaced by domestic sources to ensure sustainability. A well-managed national blood transfusion program requires a robust data collection and reporting system. Adequate national data on blood availability and safety enable countries to set priorities and strengthen their blood systems. Surveillance systems should be established to monitor the incidence and prevalence of transfusion-transmissible infections, such as HIV, HBV, and HCV, among blood donors, as well as transfusion outcomes in recipients, including post-transfusion infection risks. Clinical transfusion data are critical for monitoring practices, influencing prescribing and administration behaviors, and reducing variations in transfusion practices. Countries with partial data should consider implementing standardized systems for data collection and management at the national level. National blood transfusion services should provide greater support for information management systems and hospitals should establish mechanisms to improve data collection, donor tracking, traceability, and overall hemovigilance. The WHO survey highlights significant disparities in the availability, safety, and use of blood and blood components between developed and developing countries. Blood transfusion safety remains a concern, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, where the prevalence of transfusion-transmissible infections among donors is high, but blood screening quality and coverage are inadequate. Additionally, these countries often lack sufficient voluntary unpaid blood donors, resulting in low donation rates and high discard rates. A robust blood system that ensures access to safe and sufficient blood and blood products is a critical component of an effective healthcare system. Strengthening national blood systems is essential to ensure adequate and safe blood supplies worldwide, especially in lowand middle-income countries. While efforts have been made to collect accurate data from countries, the data submitted by national health authorities have not been independently verified. The accuracy of the data depends on the quality of the data collection systems in each country. Some countries report comprehensive national data, while others provide limited information from a subset of blood centers. Incomplete data and varying interpretations of indicators have affected the analysis of the information received. In some cases, partial data may present a more favorable picture than the reality, particularly in lowand middle-income countries where data often reflect major cities with better facilities and management, leaving poorer areas unreported. Caution should be exercised in generalizing these data. Updated indicators in this report may differ from previous WHO publications due to differences in data availability and adjustments made during validation. A higher proportion of middleand low-income countries report only reactive results for transfusion-transmissible infection testing, without confirmatory testing. Strategies and protocols for screening and confirmatory tests vary between countries, and in some cases, samples are considered positive based on repeated reactive results without additional confirmatory testing.
